messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The ambush had unfolded in a narrow, wind-scoured valley during his third year overseas, a moment that still fractures Arthur Vance’s breathing thirty-five years later. He had been moving through the jagged ravine when the sudden, deafening snap of automatic fire and the heavy thud of boots against shale broke their formation. When the dust settled, Arthur was the only one left standing among his squad mates. In the years since, the memory of that valley refused to settle into a coherent narrative. He knew exactly what had transpired, yet he would sit at his kitchen table and stare at his coffee cup, unable to find the words to describe it to his partner or to himself. The silence in his head was always followed by a rush of terror identical to the one he felt when the rifles opened up. That terror quickly curdled into a heavy, unshakable conviction that he had no right to draw his next breath while others lay dead in the dirt. He felt like a ghost in his own life, certain that the foundation of who he was had been burned away in that valley, leaving behind a man who could not recognize his own reflection. The world, he had come to believe, was an inherently dangerous place where safety was an illusion and death could strike without warning. His survival guilt and the conviction that the world remained a hostile environment ensured that the memory would never fade; instead, every quiet moment summoned the same terror he felt at the time, locking the past into the present. Because Arthur’s internal narrative framed his identity as permanently fractured and his surroundings as fundamentally unsafe, his daily life began to shrink. He stopped wearing dark, rugged field jackets or heavy wool trousers, finding the texture and color of similar clothes unbearable against his skin. He avoided going near places with steep drop-offs or confined, echoing spaces, telling himself it was merely a preference for open, flat terrain. The terror that surged in his chest whenever the valley’s geography crossed his mind convinced him that he needed to shield himself from any resemblance to the past, so he systematically avoided thinking about the event altogether. Yet, by refusing to process the memory, he only reinforced the conviction that he was fundamentally broken. Every time he turned away from a familiar texture or clamped down on a thought, the world grew marginally more dangerous in his estimation, and the guilt over surviving felt heavier than before. He was certain that the only way to stay safe was to keep moving, to keep his head down, and to never look back, even though the strategy was slowly starving him of his own peace. Arthur worked as a warehouse worker, a job that initially offered the predictable rhythm he craved, but the high ceilings and concrete aisles of the distribution center eventually became a new landscape of threat. When he walked past the loading bays on his break, the smell of heated metal and the low hum of forklifts aligned with the terrain of the ambush site, forcing him to step back and cross the street rather than face the space. His avoidance of the location had become a rigid rule, one that dictated his routes and his breathing. The guilt that accompanied the memory would not let him rest, and the terror on recall would directly feed back into his negative appraisals, convincing him once more that he was fundamentally broken and that the world was an unforgiving place. He found himself retreating into the same mental habits that had kept him alive in the valley, even as they hollowed out the life he had built. At sixty, the exhaustion of maintaining the distance finally outweighed the fear of facing the past. Arthur sat in the therapist’s office, his hands resting on his knees, wondering if it was possible to reclaim the man he used to be. He was most afraid that the terror would return with a strength he could no longer outrun, but he hoped that talking about the valley might finally give him the words he had been searching for. He wanted to stop flinching at the sound of heavy doors slamming, wanted to wear a simple jacket without waiting for his stomach to turn, and wanted to believe that he could walk through a parking lot without calculating every exit. The memory and the dread were still there, but for the first time in decades, Arthur was willing to let them sit in the room with him.
